parts.title: TypeScript for many test cases at once

blocks.text:
# Week 8, Day 2.1 — TypeScript for many test cases at once

Five concepts. Today you stop writing one test per scenario and start driving many
scenarios from one file of data.

> **Every Run starts fresh.** The studio executes your code in a new process each time, so nothing is left over between runs.

| # | Concept | Why today needs it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Arrays | Your test cases become a list. |
| 2 | `forEach` with index | One loop generates many tests. |
| 3 | Spread `...` | Copy a booking, change one field. |
| 4 | Rest in destructuring | Remove a field to test what happens. |
| 5 | Importing a JSON file | Test data lives outside the test. |

Already covered — one link each, no re-teaching: `let`/`const`, template literals, objects,
nested access, `async`/`await` and destructuring are all in
[Day 1.1](/learn/w8/d1/p1).

## 1. Arrays

A list, in square brackets. Items are reached by position, starting at **0**.

An array can hold objects — and a list of objects is exactly what "my test cases" looks like.

**Expected:** `Ada 3`, then `blank first name`, `(blank)`, `how many cases: 2`

`caseList[1]` is the *second* item. Counting from zero is the single most common off-by-one
source in test code.

**Challenge:** add a third case and print its `expected`.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 2. `forEach` with an index

Runs a function once per item. The second parameter is the position — useful for numbering
tests, because "Case 3 failed" beats "a test failed".

**Expected:**

```
Case 1 — normal booking
Case 2 — blank first name
Case 3 — long stay
```

`index + 1` because humans count from 1 and arrays count from 0.

**Where it shows up:** tomorrow's data-driven spec is this exact loop, with `test(...)`
inside instead of `console.log`.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 3. Spread `...` — copy, then change one thing

`{ ...original, field: newValue }` means "everything from original, but with this field
replaced". The original is untouched.

Negative testing is mostly this: take something valid, break exactly one part.

**Expected:** three lines — the original unchanged, then two copies each differing in one field.

Order matters: `{ firstname: "", ...validBooking }` puts the spread *last*, so `firstname`
gets overwritten back to `"Jim"`. The override has to come after.

**Challenge:** make a copy with `depositpaid` set to `false`.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 4. Rest in destructuring — remove a field

`const { firstname, ...rest } = booking` pulls `firstname` out and puts *everything else*
into `rest`. So `rest` is the booking **without** that field.

That is how you test "what happens if this is missing entirely?" — different from sending it
blank, and often a very different answer.

**Expected:** `pulled out: Jim`, `{"lastname":"Brown","totalprice":111}`, `false`

Blank (`""`) and missing are **not** the same test. Today you will find an API that accepts
one and crashes on the other.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## 5. Importing a JSON file

Test data belongs in its own file, so adding a case means editing data, not code.

```ts
import testData from "./day2-booking-data.json";
```

This works because `tsconfig.json` has `resolveJsonModule: true`. The import gives you a
normal object — no parsing step.

> Notebook cells cannot use this import form. Below is the equivalent for exploring; the
> `import` line is what goes in the real spec file.

**Expected:** `cases found: 4`, then the four case names.

If you get "No such file or directory", that file gets written by
[Day 2.2](/learn/w8/d2/p2) — run that lesson's data cell first, or just read on.

## Recap

| Concept | Remember |
|---|---|
| Arrays | Position starts at 0. |
| `forEach((item, i) => …)` | `i + 1` for human-readable numbering. |
| Spread `...` | Copy then override — override goes last. |
| Rest `{ x, ...others }` | Missing and blank are different tests. |
| JSON import | Data in a file; adding a case edits no code. |

**Next:** [Day 2.2 — Negative scenarios and data-driven tests](/learn/w8/d2/p2)

# Week 8, Day 2.2 — Testing what *shouldn't* work

Day 1 proved the happy path. Today you break things on purpose — and find four real defects
in the API you have been testing.

You will also stop copy-pasting a test per scenario, and drive many scenarios from one JSON file.

> **Mode: explore.** Write code in the editor and press Run — it drives a real browser and shows you what happened.

## Why negative testing is your job

Customers describe what should work. Nobody writes a requirement saying "and if the password
is wrong, refuse it" — so negative scenarios are designed by testers, not handed over.

Car makers don't crash-test because a buyer asked; they crash-test so the airbag works when a
buyer makes a mistake. Same reasoning, same responsibility.

| Status | Means | Whose fault |
|---|---|---|
| `400 Bad Request` | your data was malformed | yours |
| `401` / `403` | not authenticated / not allowed | yours |
| `404 Not Found` | no such thing | yours |
| `500 Internal Server Error` | the server threw | **theirs — that's a bug** |

A `500` is never an acceptable answer to bad input. A good API says `400` and explains which
field. Remember that; you are about to see one that doesn't.

## Running just one test: `test.only`

While hunting a scenario you don't want the other twenty tests in the way.

```ts
test.only("the one I am working on", async ({ request }) => { … });
```

Playwright then runs *only* that test. Two rules: it works per file, and **never commit it** —
your suite would silently shrink to one test. The root config sets `forbidOnly` under CI,
so it fails the build rather than passing quietly.

## Example 1 — a wrong password

**Objective:** log in with bad credentials and see what actually comes back.

**Expected:**

```
status: 200
token:  undefined
body:   {"reason":"Bad credentials"}
```

Two findings, and the second one is a lesson about *you*, not the API:

**The status is `200`.** A failed login is still a successfully *delivered request*. This API
reports the failure in the body. So `expect(res.status()).toBe(200)` passing tells you nothing
about whether the login worked — you have to check the body.

**Printing one field would have misled you.** `token` is `undefined`, and it's tempting to
conclude the API returns nothing at all. It returns `{"reason":"Bad credentials"}` — a perfectly
clear message you'd have missed. Print the *whole body* before drawing conclusions.

**Challenge:** try a wrong username with the right password. Same response?

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 2 — blank, and missing, are different tests

**Objective:** send a booking with an empty first name, then with no first name at all.

**Expected:**

```
blank firstname   -> 200 ""
missing firstname -> 500 Internal Server Error
```

**Two defects in three lines.**

A blank name is accepted and stored — no validation at all. And leaving the field out entirely
**crashes the server**. A `500` means the code threw an exception instead of checking its input.

This is what negative testing is for. Both would have gone unnoticed forever by happy-path tests.

**What to do at work:** raise these as defects. Do not soften the test to match the bug — a test
asserting `500` documents that the crash is known, which is honest. A test that skips the case
pretends it never happened.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 3 — the quiet one

**Objective:** send a price that isn't a number.

**Expected:** `200`, `totalprice: null`, `firstname: Jim`

This is the worst of the four. The request **succeeds**, the booking is created, and the price
is silently thrown away and replaced with `null`. No error, no warning.

A customer's booking exists with no price attached. Nothing in a happy-path suite would ever
catch it — and neither would a human clicking through the UI, because they'd type a number.

**Challenge:** try `depositpaid: "yes"` instead of `true`. Does it survive?

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Example 4 — why parsing a delete blows up

**Objective:** find out what a delete actually returns.

Day 1 checked the status code of a delete and moved on. Look closer.

**Expected:**

```
status: 201
body:   "Created" | length: 7
JSON.parse THREW: Unexpected token 'C', "Created" is not valid JSON
```

The body is seven characters of plain text — **not JSON**. So calling `.json()` on a delete
throws, and the error message points at JSON parsing rather than at your real mistake.

**The rule:** a response with no content has nothing to parse. Check the status, read `.text()`
if you're curious, and don't reach for `.json()` out of habit.

If you ever see `Unexpected token … is not valid JSON` right after a delete, this is why.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## The same four checks, as a real spec

`console.log` showed you the behaviour. A test has to assert it — including asserting that a
`500` happens, which is how a known defect gets documented rather than forgotten.

> ▶ **Run it yourself:** `npx playwright test week8/generated/day2-negative.spec.ts`

**Expected:** `7 passed`.

Note the last assertion:

```ts
await expect(del.json()).rejects.toThrow();
```

`rejects` is how you assert that something fails. Testing that the wrong thing breaks is as
legitimate as testing that the right thing works.

## Now the duplication problem

You have four negative cases. A real create-booking form has six fields, so blank-each-field
alone is six more tests — and each is the same request with one value changed.

Copy-pasting the test six times gives you six places to update when the endpoint moves. That is
**code duplication**, and it is the difference between a suite people maintain and one they
abandon.

The fix: the *test* is one thing, the *data* is a list. Put the list in a file.

**Expected:** three numbered lines.

Now swap `console.log` for `test(...)` and each case becomes a **real, separately-named test**
with its own pass/fail and its own retry. That is the whole trick.

The loop runs while Playwright is *collecting* tests, before any of them execute — which is why
this produces four tests rather than one test that loops four times. One failure doesn't hide
the other three.

## Data in a file, tests generated from it

The cell below writes the data file and the spec, then runs it.

> ▶ **Run it yourself:** `npx playwright test week8/generated/day2-data-driven.spec.ts`

**Expected:** `4 passed`, named `Case 1 — a normal booking` through `Case 4 — NEGATIVE …`.

**Add a fifth scenario by editing the JSON file and nothing else.** No new test, no copy-paste.
That is the payoff.

Two details worth copying into your own work:

- The expected result lives **in the data file** (`expectedStatus`, `expectedFirstname`), so a
  negative case sits alongside the positive ones instead of needing its own test.
- Assertions compare against `testCase.booking.…`, never against a value typed a second time.
  Typing `"Ada"` twice means a typo makes the test pass for the wrong reason.

## Best practices

- **Break one thing at a time.** Spread from a known-good object so a failure has one cause.
- **Blank ≠ missing ≠ wrong type.** Three different tests, and today all three behaved differently.
- **Assert the real behaviour**, then raise the defect. Never soften a test to make a bug pass.
- **Print the whole body** before concluding an API returns nothing.
- **`test.only` never gets committed.**

## Common mistakes

| You see | Usually means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Unexpected token … is not valid JSON` | parsed a body with no content | check status; use `.text()` |
| Only one test ran | a stray `test.only` | remove it |
| All cases pass suspiciously | you asserted a hardcoded value, not the data | compare against `testCase.…` |
| `500` from bad input | a server-side defect | raise it; assert it so it's documented |
| Spread didn't override | the spread came last | `{ ...base, field: value }` |

**Next:** [Day 2.3](/learn/w8/d2/p3) — where this data lives once the suite is real.

# Week 8, Day 2.3 — Test data that scales

Same data-driven idea as [Day 2.2](/learn/w8/d2/p2). No new API. The change is **where the data
lives and what shape it has** once a suite has hundreds of cases.

## What breaks first

A raw JSON file is right for four cases. Watch what happens as it grows:

| Problem at scale | Why it hurts |
|---|---|
| Every case repeats all six fields | 40 cases means 40 copies of `bookingdates`; one format change is 40 edits |
| A typo in a field name is silent | `frstname` in JSON is not a compile error — the test just fails oddly |
| No types | Nothing stops `totalprice: "free"` reaching the request |
| Cases share mutable objects | One test's edit leaks into another's data |

The fix is the same instinct as Day 1.3's API client: **name the knowledge once**. Here that
means a **type** for the shape and a **factory** for the defaults.

**Expected:** the default booking, then one with a blank name and zero price — everything else
still filled in.

Compare the two ways of writing a case:

| JSON file | Factory |
|---|---|
| all six fields, every time | `aBooking({ firstname: "" })` |
| typo fails at runtime, confusingly | typo fails at compile time |
| shared object, mutable | fresh object per call |

The line that matters is `...overrides` **last** — the same rule from Day 2.1. Put it first and
your overrides get silently reset to the defaults.

## Cases as a typed table

With a factory, a case is a name plus what makes it different. The whole suite fits on a screen
and reads like a specification.

**Expected:** four numbered lines.

Each case now says only what is *interesting* about it. `aBooking({ totalprice: 0 })` reads as
"a normal booking, except free" — which is what the tester actually meant.

## When to keep the JSON file anyway

Types and factories are not always right. Choose by **who edits the data**:

| Use a factory | Use a JSON/CSV file |
|---|---|
| Testers own the data | Non-developers contribute cases |
| Cases differ by one or two fields | Every case is genuinely different |
| You want compile-time safety | Data is exported from another system |
| Data lives with the tests | Data changes without a code release |

Many real suites use both: JSON for a bulk table exported by the business, a factory for the
handful of edge cases engineers add.

Whichever you pick, one rule does not bend: **the expected result travels with the input.** A
case that says what to send but not what should happen is not a test case.

## What a reviewer checks

- **No expected value typed twice** — assert against the case data, not a repeated literal.
- **Every case independently named**, so a failure report says which one.
- **A fresh object per case** — no shared mutable data between tests.
- **Negative cases sit with positive ones**, not in a separate forgotten file.
- **No `test.only`** anywhere.
- **Known defects asserted, not skipped** — a test pinning the `500` is documentation.

**Next:** [Day 2.4](/learn/w8/d2/p4) — your turn.

# Week 8, Day 2.4 — Practice

Three problems. No answer key — each says how to check yourself.

Target: **Restful Booker** — `https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com`
([docs](https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/apidoc/index.html)), credentials `admin` / `password123`.

> Stuck past twenty minutes? The gap is in [Day 2.1](/learn/w8/d2/p1) or [Day 2.2](/learn/w8/d2/p2).

## When you're done

**Which of the four defects from Day 2.2 would a user actually notice?** The silent
`totalprice: null` is the dangerous one — no error, no clue, wrong data. Ranking findings by
user impact is most of what makes a bug report worth reading.

**Next:** [Day 3.1](/learn/w8/d3/p1) — pulling data straight out of a page.

problems.statement:
**Build.** Find out how this API handles two more kinds of bad input.

1. Send a booking where `bookingdates.checkout` is *before* `checkin`
2. Send a booking where `totalprice` is negative

For each: print the status and the whole response body, then write one sentence on whether the
behaviour is acceptable.

**Check yourself.** You can state, from evidence, whether each is a defect. "It returned 200 and
stored a negative price" is a finding. "It seemed fine" is not.

> **Hint** — print the whole body. One field would have hidden `"reason":"Bad credentials"` in
> Day 2.2.

**Build.** A data-driven spec covering **every field** of a booking left blank.

A booking has six fields. Build one spec that, for each field, sends an otherwise-valid booking
with just that field blanked, and records what happens.

1. Data in a file or a typed array — your choice, but each case names the field it breaks
2. One test generated per case, named so a failure says which field
3. Expected status stored **with** each case

**Where.** A spec in `week8/generated/`.

**Check yourself.** Six separately-named tests appear in the output. Adding a seventh field means
editing data only — if you had to touch the test body, the data isn't doing the work.

> **Hint** — a factory plus `Partial<Booking>` makes each case one line. Some fields will
> surprise you; assert what actually happens.

**Build.** Negative coverage on top of Day 1.3's `BookingApi` client.

1. Extend the client with a `signInWith(username, password)` that does **not** assume success
2. Add a `createRaw(body: unknown)` so a test can send deliberately malformed data — the typed
   `create()` cannot, by design
3. A fixture supplying the client
4. Tests covering: bad credentials, a missing field, a wrong type, and an update with an expired
   or invented token

**Constraints — these are the exercise:**

- **No `expect()` inside the client.** A client that asserts success cannot test failure.
- **Each test names the defect it documents**, e.g. `"missing firstname crashes the server (known defect)"`.
- Every test must pass **run on its own**.

**Check yourself.** Run three times in a row — all pass every time. Then ask: if the API were
fixed tomorrow to return `400` instead of `500`, how many tests fail, and is that the right number?

> **Hint** — `createRaw` taking `unknown` rather than `Booking` is the interesting design
> decision. Think about why the type-safe method should stay type-safe.
